newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto says Pakistan government could collapse.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto says Pakistan government could collapse.

text.p: Pakistani opposition leader Benazir Bhutto said on Saturday that Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's four-month-old government could collapse prematurely and appeared to be borrowing time by taking populist measures.

In an interview with Reuters, the former prime minister attacked the economic performance of the present government, which blames her three previous years in office for an economic crisis, and said she feared it would increase the budget deficit and inflation.

"I think this government doesn't believe that it is going to last," Bhutto said. "It's borrowing time and it's borrowing money (for state expenses). It is trying to take populist measures so that when it actually collapses people will not be in such turmoil."

She was referring to various tax concessions and economic reform packages announced by Sharif's government since taking office in February for a five-year term after a landslide election victory against Bhutto.
She said inflation and unemployment were on the rise in Pakistan because of the failure of Sharif's government to take measures to put the economy on track.

The government has imposed no new taxes in the budget for fiscal 1997/98 (July/June) announced earlier this month, and Bhutto wondered how it would meet a higher outlay and achieve a promised reduction in budget deficit.
"Last year we announced a budget of 500 billion rupees ($12.34 billion) and this year they have announced a budget of 550 billion rupees," Bhutto said.

"But they have announced many tax cuts and reliefs,... refused to document the economy, and treated tax payers and tax evaders at par," she said referring to a scheme allowing an amnesty for concealed assets.
If the government does not provide for an additional 50 billion rupees and gives concessions, "where on earth is the money going to come from to fill the gap?", Bhutto asked.

She said the budget deficit in 1997/98 could rise to nine percent compared to a government plan to bring it down to five percent of the gross domestic product (GDP) from an estimated 6.2 percent in 1996/97.

She denied charges of corruption being levelled against her and her detained husband by Sharif's government and said authorities had still not brought any formal charges eight months after President Farooq Leghari sacked her government on disputed charges of misrule.
She accused the government of arresting and pressuring govenrment officials to testify against her.

"Todate... not a single charge of corruption has been made against me or my husband," Bhutto said. "Instead people have been arrested, persecuted, coerced, perssured, denied their salaries, bankrupted by hiring lawyers and they are asked to turn approvers by lying against us.
"I guess no charges will be made until they manage to hound some of the people into psychologically and mentally falling apart and be prepared to commit perjury."
